history: The Autódromo José Carlos Pace, more commonly known as Interlagos, has been a staple of Brazilian motorsport since its inception in 1940. Originally sprawling over nearly 8 kilometers, the circuit was significantly shortened in the 1990s due to safety concerns and the increasing demands of modern racing. While the 'Classic' layout retains the essence of the modern Grand Prix circuit, it represents the track's configuration following these crucial changes. It is the layout used for major international events like Formula 1. The track is named in honor of Brazilian Formula 1 driver José Carlos Pace, who tragically died in a plane crash in 1977. Interlagos has hosted countless iconic races and witnessed some of motorsport's most dramatic moments.
atmosphere: The roar of the crowd reverberates through the grandstands, a wave of sound that crashes over the track as the cars hurtle through the Senna S. The air is thick with anticipation, the smell of burning rubber and high-octane fuel mingling with the vibrant energy of the Brazilian fans. Confetti rains down as a local driver battles for position, the iconic Interlagos skyline a backdrop to the thrilling spectacle. The passion of the 'torcida' is palpable, making every lap an unforgettable experience.
trackCharacter: The 'Classic' layout of Interlagos is a demanding, undulating circuit that rewards bravery and precision. Its anti-clockwise direction, coupled with a mix of high-speed straights and tight, technical corners, presents a unique challenge for drivers and engineers alike. The constant elevation changes, particularly in the first sector, require a car with excellent balance and strong engine performance. The track's abrasive surface also puts a premium on tire management, making strategy a crucial element of success.

famousCorners.name: Senna S
famousCorners.description: The most famous corner complex at Interlagos, it’s a high-speed left-right-left sequence that demands commitment and precision.
famousCorners.challenge: Maintaining momentum and avoiding compromising the exit, crucial for the following straight.

famousCorners.name: Curva do Sol
famousCorners.description: A long, sweeping right-hander that follows the Senna S, it's a vital corner for setting up overtaking opportunities into the Descida do Lago.
famousCorners.challenge: Finding the optimal line to maximize speed and prepare for the braking zone ahead.

famousCorners.name: Descida do Lago
famousCorners.description: A steep downhill section leading into a tricky left-hander. The braking zone is critical.
famousCorners.challenge: Managing the weight transfer under braking and avoiding locking up the wheels on the descent.

famousCorners.name: Junção
famousCorners.description: A tight, technical left-hander that links the infield section to the long run up the hill towards the start/finish line.
famousCorners.challenge: Maintaining good traction and carrying enough speed through the corner to set up a strong exit onto the main straight.

famousCorners.name: Subida dos Boxes
famousCorners.description: A long, uphill straight after Junção, leading back to the start/finish line. It provides a crucial opportunity for overtaking with DRS.
famousCorners.challenge: Maximizing engine power and aerodynamic efficiency to gain an advantage on the run to the braking zone.

keyFactors: Engine power, especially on the uphill sections
Aerodynamic efficiency for the straights and high-speed corners
Braking stability for the Descida do Lago and other heavy braking zones
Tire management due to the abrasive track surface
overtakingSpots: End of the main straight (Subida dos Boxes) after the DRS zone
Into Turn 1 (Senna S), a risky but potentially rewarding maneuver
Into Turn 4 (Descida do Lago), requiring late braking and precision
Exit of Junção onto the Subida dos Boxes, if a driver can get a good run out of the corner.
historySnippets: Interlagos was built on swampland, hence its name ('between lakes').
The original Interlagos circuit was over 8 kilometers long.
Ayrton Senna won twice at Interlagos, in 1991 and 1993.
The circuit's elevation changes are among the most dramatic in Formula 1.
The abrasive track surface is known for causing high tire wear.
Interlagos is one of the few major circuits that runs in an anti-clockwise direction.
weatherNotes: Interlagos is notorious for its unpredictable weather. Sudden rain showers are common, often turning the race into a strategic lottery. The track's elevation changes can also lead to localized variations in grip levels, making tire choice and setup even more critical. The asphalt dries quickly, so intermediate tires are frequently used.
drivingAdvice: To be fast at Interlagos, you need to be aggressive but precise. Carry as much speed as possible through the Senna S, but be mindful of the exit. Nail the braking point for the Descida do Lago, and get a good run out of the Junção to maximize your speed up the hill towards the start/finish line. Tire management is key, so avoid overdriving the car in the early stages of the race.
famousRaces: 1991 Brazilian Grand Prix: Ayrton Senna, struggling with a failing gearbox, heroically held off Riccardo Patrese to win his first home race.
2003 Brazilian Grand Prix: A chaotic race marred by heavy rain and multiple crashes, eventually won by Giancarlo Fisichella after a lengthy red flag period.
2008 Brazilian Grand Prix: Felipe Massa won the race, but Lewis Hamilton secured the World Championship by overtaking Timo Glock on the final corner of the final lap.
localCulture: São Paulo is a vibrant, bustling metropolis, and the atmosphere around Interlagos during race week is electric. Fans flock to the circuit from all over Brazil and South America, bringing with them a passion for motorsport that is unmatched. The local cuisine is diverse, with churrascarias (barbecue restaurants) being particularly popular. The paddock is a hive of activity, with teams and drivers enjoying the warm hospitality of the Brazilian people.
